cards.explanation: The answer is in righteousness. Isaiah says it right up front: “Behold, a king will reign in righteousness…” That's how this king rules, and it's the whole point. Not by looking impressive, not by being the loudest guy in the room. He reigns the right way, every time.

The answer is justice, friends. Isaiah says the king reigns in righteousness and the princes rule with justice. Righteousness at the top and justice right behind it. That's a leadership team I'd sign up for.

The answer is in a dry land. Isaiah says each ruler will be like “streams of water in a dry land, like the shadow of a great rock in an arid land.” I think water and shade mean the most exactly where there isn't any. Think of how good shade feels after a long stretch in a hot kitchen standing next to the oven.
The answer is True. Isaiah says the ears of those who hear will listen. Hearing and listening are two different things, friends. I've heard my kitchen timer go off plenty of times and did NOT listen.

The answer is False. Isaiah says the mind of the rash will know and understand. The same verse says the stammering tongue will speak clearly and fluently. Rushing in without thinking is something I know a lot about, so this verse makes me smile.

The word is fool. Isaiah says no longer will a fool be called noble, nor a scoundrel be respected. It comes after Isaiah says a king will reign in righteousness (verse 1). That's a kingdom I'd like to see.

The answer is the hungry. Isaiah says the fool “…leaves the hungry empty and deprives the thirsty of drink.” That's a fool who leaves people in need with nothing. Isaiah doesn't soften it, and neither will I.

The answer is False. Isaiah says the scoundrel hatches plots to destroy the poor with lies, “…even when the plea of the needy is just.” Even when. His weapons are destructive, Isaiah says. This is a heavy verse, so I'll just say it plainly: the plea is fair, and he still goes after them.

The word is worthy. Isaiah says the noble man makes honorable plans and “…stands up for worthy causes.” Honorable plans and worthy causes go together in that verse. That's a short sentence with a lot of backbone.

The answer is in just over a year. Isaiah says “In a little more than a year you will tremble, O secure ones.” That's not some far-off day. A year and a bit goes by quick, especially when you're comfortable.
The word is fail. Isaiah says the grape harvest will fail, and the fruit harvest will not arrive. That's a hard year for anyone counting on the vines. Nothing in the verse softens it.

The answer is the pleasant fields and the fruitful vines. Isaiah says “Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vines…” The land itself is what they're mourning. When the harvest goes, that's a loss you can see.

The answer is False. Isaiah says “…the palace will be forsaken, the busy city abandoned.” The hill and the watchtower become caves, and wild donkeys and flocks move in. A busy city gone quiet is a hard picture.

The answer is the Spirit. Isaiah says the ruin lasts “…until the Spirit is poured out upon us from on high.” That one word turns the whole thing around. After the Spirit is poured out, the desert becomes an orchard.

The answer is True. Isaiah says that once the Spirit is poured out, “…the desert will be an orchard…” Dry ground becomes a place full of fruit. And then he adds that the orchard will seem like a forest.

The word is wilderness. Isaiah says “Then justice will inhabit the wilderness, and righteousness will dwell in the fertile field.” The wild, empty place gets justice, and the fertile field gets righteousness. Both places get named.
The word is peace. Isaiah says “The work of righteousness will be peace…” And the service of righteousness will be quiet confidence forever. Doing right ends up in a calm place.

The answer is False. Isaiah says “…my people will dwell in a peaceful place, in safe and secure places of rest.” They settle in, with safe and secure places of rest. It's the kind of rest I'd take over a hundred cookie orders.

The answer is those who sow beside abundant waters. That's how Isaiah ends: “Blessed are those who sow beside abundant waters…” Sowing near plenty of water is a smart place to plant, and Isaiah calls those people blessed. And it follows the picture of the Spirit poured out and the land changed.
